nameStory: The narrow-leaved arrowhead gets its name from its slender, grass-like leaves that are much thinner than its famous cousin, the broadleaf arrowhead. While most arrowheads have the classic arrow-shaped leaves we expect, this little rebel decided to go minimal with thin, needle-like foliage. It's also called 'awl-leaf' arrowhead because its leaves resemble an awl - a pointed tool used for making holes.
description: Narrow-leaved arrowhead is a small aquatic plant that breaks all the rules of what you'd expect an arrowhead to look like. Instead of the classic arrow-shaped leaves, this petite water plant sports thin, grass-like leaves that emerge directly from underwater roots. It's one of the smaller members of the arrowhead family, staying compact and low to the water surface. You'll find it growing completely submerged or with just its flower stalks poking above the waterline.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thin, grass-like leaves that feel smooth and ribbon-like between your fingers - completely unlike the broad arrow shape of other arrowheads

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with three rounded petals held on thin stalks above the water surface, appearing delicate and papery to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stays small and compact, often completely underwater except for flowering stalks, forming dense colonies from creeping underwater roots

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: All leaves arise directly from the base - no stem leaves - and they sway gently underwater like green ribbons in the current

habitat: Look for narrow-leaved arrowhead in shallow, quiet waters of ponds, slow streams, and marshy areas throughout New England. It prefers sandy or muddy bottoms in water that's typically 6 inches to 3 feet deep. You'll often find it growing alongside other aquatic plants like pondweeds and water lilies in areas with gentle water movement.

seasonality.spring: New grass-like leaves emerge underwater from overwintered roots, creating fresh green ribbons beneath the surface. Early growth is entirely submerged.
seasonality.summer: Flowering period when small white blooms appear on thin stalks above water. This is the best time for identification as the contrast between narrow leaves and typical arrowhead flowers is most obvious.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants begin to die back, with leaves becoming less prominent. Seeds mature and disperse in the water.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground roots and rhizomes, leaving no visible trace above the sediment until spring returns.

funFact: This tiny arrowhead is like the shapeshifter of the water plant world - it can grow completely different leaf forms depending on whether it's submerged, floating, or stranded on mudflats, sometimes producing heart-shaped leaves that look nothing like its typical grass-like foliage!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with grass-leaved arrowhead, but narrow-leaved arrowhead's leaves are even thinner and more delicate. It can also be mistaken for various pondweeds or even aquatic grasses, but the distinctive three-petaled white flowers in summer are the dead giveaway - no grass or pondweed produces these classic arrowhead blooms.
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, this is one of our rarest arrowheads and might be easily overlooked because it looks so un-arrowhead-like. Many botanists consider it more of a southern species that just barely reaches into our region, making any sighting quite special.
compareHints: Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead. While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has strap-like foliage, narrow-leaved arrowhead's leaves are almost thread-like. It's also much smaller overall than most of its relatives, rarely growing more than a few inches tall above water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
